title: ‘My Whole Life Has Been the Audition’: Jake Shears Talks ‘Rocky Horror,’ Tim Curry & His ‘One Request’ About Callbacks
summary: The Scissor Sisters rocker currently stars as Dr. Frank-N-Furter on Broadway.
contentText:
Although fans have been cosplaying as Dr. Frank-N-Furter for half a century thanks to The Rocky Horror Picture Show ’s infamous midnight screenings, stepping into the mad scientist’s spangled heels remains a tall order for one reason: Tim Curry. Both on stage and on screen ( The Rocky Horror Show debuted on London’s West End in 1973; the Jim Sharman-directed film released in 1975), Curry used his mellifluous voice, wildcat mannerisms and wicked wit to craft one of the most unforgettable characters of all time.

Related

It’s Astounding, Time Is Fleeting: 50 Years of ‘Rocky Horror’ Coverage In Our Back Pages

Tony Winner Sam Pinkleton on His ‘No A–holes’ Policy for ‘The Rocky Horror Show’ on Broadway

Suki Waterhouse, Australian Crawl Join Sydney Opera House's On The Steps Series

Curry’s Frank was easy to swallow but tough to follow — many who have laced up the corset since then have glimmered, but always in Curry’s shadow. When Jake Shears became the third actor to portray Frank-N-Furter in the current Broadway revival of The Rocky Horror Show at Studio 54, his debut took on a sad, sweet resonance, happening just weeks after Curry’s death at age 80. (Curry passed away on Aug. 25; Shears debuted on Sept. 11, taking over from Paul Soileau, who followed Luke Evans’ Tony-nominated turn.)

“If you’d told me when I was 15 that I’d be in the theater rehearsing for it on the day [Curry’s death] happened — to be able to share that moment with everyone else and be in the theater even now — it feels like a living memorial in a way,” Shears tells Billboard .

It may be a living memorial, but don’t get it twisted: this version of the sci-fi/horror/musical is no hushed, reverent recreation. Directed by Tony winner Sam Pinkleton ( Oh, Mary!, Ta-Da! ), this production leans into DIY set design, hodgepodge casting and playful camp to reanimate a show that remains as transgressive and titillating as ever. Eight times a week at Studio 54, the Scissor Sisters rocker-turned-actor brings his sly, bratty take on the Sweet Transvestite from Transsexual Transylvania to life.

As he packed his go-to bag ahead of a Tuesday night performance, Shears spoke to Billboard about his lifelong obsession with Rocky Horror, what he thinks about the audience callbacks and how Curry’s death affected his take on the role.  

What’s your backstory with Rocky Horror ? Is this something that’s been with you throughout your whole life?

I’m a true Rocky Horror nerd. I don’t think there would be Scissor Sisters without Rocky Horror . I don’t know if I would be a performer without Rocky Horror . I discovered it for myself when I was 12, just about to turn 13. For its 15th anniversary in 1990, they were putting it out on VHS. In celebration of that — I was an avid MTV and VH1 watcher at that age — I started seeing imagery from it and became really, really curious.

Right — it was a late arrival to VHS and a big thing when it finally came out.

My mom wouldn’t let me watch it, and it became a real point of contention between us. So my parents went out of town, and my older sister got me the soundtrack of the original Roxy cast from Los Angeles. That was the first time I heard the songs. Then when my parents were out of town, my sister got me the VHS tape, so I got to see the film for the first time and it just blew my mind. I immediately started figuring out ways to go to the Saturday night screenings, and I became obsessed with it. I’ve always been obsessed with it. It’s always been a part of my fantasies. I think it’s the greatest movie ever made. I think it’s the greatest musical ever made. There’s something about the script, the story — it is so magical.

It really is unlike anything else.

This may be a digression, but Rocky Horror feels to me like a theme park ride. There’s so much going on in it, and there’s this underlying story happening underneath that you only get glimmers of. There’s something about the show that really spurs your imagination on. Your brain fills in so many blanks in Rocky Horror . I think that’s one of the reasons it’s touched so many people. I love that it’s kind of amoral.

The combination of all those things really affected me as a 13-year-old. It was also my first sort of dawning — it was my first “it gets better.” In my book [ Boys Keep Swinging ] I wrote about it like a message in a bottle, saying, “Hey, we’re out here.” It was like a message from my future. To me, it’s a sacred text. It’s my Rosetta Stone. Getting to do it [on Broadway] is a really deep, deep thing for me. I still kind of can’t believe it, and I don’t know if I’ll ever do anything that will make me as happy as what I’m doing now.

That’s beautiful: 12, 13 is such a formative age. To grow up with that, have it inform your outlook and then step into the heels. How do you top that?

There isn’t a way to top it. The other fun thing is that I love theater so much, and I love the repetition of it — the absolute grind of it. When you’re doing a five-show weekend, the whole thing turns into one big funhouse mirror. It gets weird. It really does put you in another kind of reality, and getting to do that in this world, with this show, feels like getting to step off the ride at Pirates of the Caribbean and go snoop around the animatronics.

That’s a great way of describing it. When they reached out to you for the role, how did that work? Did you have to do an audition?

I think my whole life has been the audition. But no — I got a call from a producer friend I’ve worked with, who said, “The Rocky Horror folks are looking for you. Do you want me to give them your number?” And I said, “Yes, yes, please.”

I was super secretive and kept it really close because it was such an exciting prospect. I had to protect myself — I could potentially be absolutely devastated if it didn’t go the right way. I’d been sitting around in London so jealous that it was happening in New York. Everyone got an earful around my kitchen table about how badly I wanted it. I was having a lot of FOMO that it even existed. A lot of my close friends were weirded out by the whole thing, because it felt like something I’d put out into the universe and then the universe hit me up.

As you were preparing for the role — between the announcement and your official stage debut — Tim Curry died. Did that change your preparation? Did it change your relationship to the role?

It did a little bit, yeah. It made me not be in denial that Tim Curry has always been in my DNA. It’s always been in my bones. So it’s made me not be super scared of that. I’ve definitely got my own spin on it. But I’m also not afraid to deliver his versions of the songs. There’s no escaping that.

They’re so iconic. But your performance does have its own flavor.

[ Joking ] The flavor is called cocaine.

[ Laughs .] How else do you do eight shows a week?

No, no — I just mean I’ve had a lot of fun thinking about the fact that we’re in Studio 54. I’m paying my respects to the ghosts at 54. We’ve got the moon in there. The spoon’s not there, but that’s been a part of the development of my Frank — Frank is really partying during this night. It’s been really fun to dig in and shape that. Please don’t write that I’m a cocaine addict.

Let the record state that you are simply making a reference to Studio 54’s snowy past, not talking about your own habits. You’re doing so many performances in such a short time. There’s that element of exhaustion, but you are going full force at the same time.

Yes. That’s the fun thing — you get to “Wild and Untamed Thing” at…
